Pregnancy

Possible causes of stillbirth and what tests can explain

Updated: November 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

After a stillbirth, wanting to understand why your baby died is natural. A review may find a likely cause, several contributing problems or no clear explanation. A condition on a list is not proof that it caused your baby’s death. This guide explains the main possibilities and the limits of testing; your team should interpret the findings together and make time for your questions.

First distinguish stillbirth from death after birth

Stillbirth means that a baby dies before or during birth and is born without signs of life. Gestational thresholds vary: US reporting commonly starts at 20 weeks, while UK guidance uses 24 completed weeks. A baby born alive who dies during the first day has had a neonatal death, not a stillbirth.

Being born before 37 weeks is called preterm birth. Prematurity can be part of a complicated pregnancy and can affect survival after a live birth, but it is not by itself an explanation for every stillbirth. The timing, signs of life at birth and underlying clinical findings need to be considered separately.

A cause, a contributor and a risk factor are different

A cause explains how the death occurred. A contributor may have helped create the conditions for it, while a risk factor is associated with a higher average chance across a population. More than one problem can be present. Having diabetes, a small baby or an infection does not, on its own, establish the cause in an individual pregnancy.

There is no single percentage that describes all stillbirth causes worldwide. Findings change with gestational age, the population, available tests and how deaths are classified. Even a thorough review may remain inconclusive. An unexplained result does not mean that nothing happened or that you caused the loss by failing to notice a symptom.

Placental function and restricted growth

The placenta transfers oxygen and nutrients between the maternal and fetal circulations. Problems with its development, blood flow or function can limit the supply a baby receives. Placental disease is an important possible contributor to stillbirth and can occur alongside high blood pressure or other pregnancy complications. Examination after birth may reveal changes that help explain the clinical picture.

Fetal growth restriction means a baby has not reached its expected growth potential; it is not the same as simply being small. Some small babies are healthy, and restricted growth can also involve infection or a fetal condition. During pregnancy, growth trends, blood-flow scans and other checks help assess concern. After a loss, size alone cannot prove placental failure or determine the cause.

Placental abruption and bleeding

Placental abruption happens when part or all of the placenta separates from the womb before birth. This can reduce the baby’s oxygen supply and cause serious maternal bleeding. Abdominal injury, high blood pressure and other factors can increase the risk, but an abruption can also happen without an obvious trigger. It is different from a placenta that is simply low in the womb.

Possible symptoms include sudden or persistent abdominal or back pain, tenderness, frequent contractions and vaginal bleeding. Bleeding may be concealed, so little visible blood does not exclude a serious problem. Seek immediate maternity assessment for these symptoms. Severe pain, heavy bleeding, faintness or collapse needs emergency help; do not wait for all the signs or drive yourself.

Maternal health conditions need individual interpretation

High blood pressure and pre-eclampsia can affect placental function and fetal growth, and severe disease can endanger both parent and baby. Pre-eclampsia usually develops after 20 weeks and may initially be detected at routine checks. Severe headache, visual changes, pain below the ribs, sudden swelling or feeling very unwell needs immediate assessment, including after birth.

Diabetes present before pregnancy and diabetes first diagnosed during pregnancy have different histories, but both need appropriate care. Gestational diabetes is associated with pregnancy complications, while stillbirth is rare and most affected pregnancies have healthy babies. Treatment and monitoring reduce risk without guaranteeing an outcome. A diabetes diagnosis should not be used to assign a cause or blame without reviewing the rest of the evidence.

Cholestasis is assessed using more than itching alone

Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy is a liver condition associated with itching and raised bile acids in the blood. The level of risk is not the same for every affected pregnancy: bile-acid results, gestational age and other circumstances matter. Specialist guidance identifies a substantially greater stillbirth risk with very high bile acids, which affects birth planning.

Report new persistent itching, particularly on the palms or soles or without a rash, to your maternity team so it can arrange assessment. Itching alone does not diagnose cholestasis or show that a baby has been harmed. Do not start a liver remedy or decide the timing of birth yourself. This condition needs its own testing and care plan.

Infections can affect the baby in different ways

Some infections can reach the womb from the vagina, such as group B streptococcus or E. coli; others can spread through the bloodstream. Infection may affect the fetus directly, damage placental function or cause serious maternal illness. Examples considered in a stillbirth review include listeriosis, syphilis, cytomegalovirus and parvovirus B19, with other organisms relevant to particular exposures or settings.

Rubella, toxoplasmosis, malaria and Q fever are among other recognized concerns, but a long infection list does not mean equal risks or that every exposure leads to loss. The illness, timing, treatment and evidence of fetal or placental involvement matter. For example, CDC reports reassuring birth outcomes when Lyme disease is appropriately treated. Fever, rash, significant illness or a concerning exposure warrants prompt clinical advice rather than self-treatment.

Genetic and developmental conditions

Some stillbirths involve a chromosome change, a genetic condition or a major developmental difference. These can affect the baby directly or occur alongside restricted growth or placental abnormalities. A finding is interpreted in the context of the examination, pregnancy scans and family history; an unusual feature alone is not a complete diagnosis.

Genetic evaluation may include a test such as a chromosome microarray, selected with the appropriate consent and specialist advice. Tissue examination and genetic testing answer different questions; neither is a universal test for every possible mutation. If a relevant result is found, genetic counselling can explain what it means for the family and any future pregnancy, without promising that recurrence can always be prevented.

Cord findings need supporting evidence

A cord prolapse or another event that significantly interrupts blood flow can threaten the baby’s oxygen supply. However, a cord loop around the neck or a knot found after birth does not automatically establish the cause of death. Such findings also occur in live births. They need careful interpretation rather than an immediate label of a cord accident.

The team looks for evidence that blood flow was actually obstructed and considers other explanations. Similarly, bleeding before or during birth can have several sources. In some cases a substantial amount of fetal blood enters the maternal circulation, causing fetal anaemia. Clinical history, placental examination and selected tests help distinguish these situations; the appearance of the cord or visible bleeding alone is insufficient.

Movement changes are a warning sign, not a cause

Reduced movement can be a sign that a baby needs assessment; it does not itself cause stillbirth or prove that death has occurred. If movements are less than usual, stop or change from the familiar pattern, call your midwife or maternity unit immediately, even at night. Do not wait until the next day or for a scheduled appointment.

A sweet drink, lying down for two hours or reaching a target of eight or ten movements cannot establish that everything is well when the usual pattern has changed. Do not use a home Doppler for reassurance. The team decides which checks are needed. If you have already lost your baby, not having noticed a warning sign does not establish personal responsibility.

What an evaluation may explain

The review usually brings together the pregnancy and medical history, examination of the placenta and cord, assessment of the baby and an offer of genetic testing and postmortem examination. Some blood tests are selected for the circumstances. Ask what each test might show, its limitations and what consent is needed. This is more than sending one tissue sample to a laboratory.

A result can identify a likely cause, suggest a contributor or remain uncertain. Tests should be chosen thoughtfully rather than assuming a large infection or clotting panel will answer every question. Arrange a follow-up discussion in plain language and ask which findings are certain, which are possible and whether any change future care. Support remains appropriate even when there is no definitive answer.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

ACOG/SMFM and RCOG recommend interpreting clinical, placental, fetal and genetic information together; a definite cause may remain unknown.

Fetal growth restriction differs from healthy small size, and a cord loop or knot alone should not be assumed to explain a death.

Urgent symptoms take priority over investigating causes online. Changed movements need immediate maternity contact.

How BeMama can help

Use this guide to prepare questions for a results appointment: what is established, what remains uncertain and what could change care. BeMama cannot interpret pathology or genetic results or determine why your baby died.

When to seek help

Call maternity care immediately for changed or reduced fetal movements, suspected fluid loss, bleeding or pre-eclampsia symptoms. Severe abdominal pain, heavy bleeding, collapse or breathing difficulty needs emergency help. Do not wait for a movement count or drive yourself in an emergency.

Evidence notes updated: November 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Stillbirth is different from a death after a baby has been born alive.
  • Placental, maternal, infectious, genetic and cord factors may contribute; a diagnosis or finding alone does not prove the cause.
  • Not every small baby is growth restricted, and not every cord loop explains a death.
  • Changed or reduced movements need immediate maternity contact, without a home reassurance test.
  • Investigation can guide understanding and future care, but an inconclusive result is possible and is not a reason for blame.

Frequently asked questions

What is the most common cause of stillbirth?

Placental problems are an important category, but the proportion and leading causes vary between populations and gestational ages. There is no universal figure that identifies the cause for one family. Some deaths remain unexplained despite a careful evaluation.

Should I count movements before calling for help?

If your baby is moving less, has stopped or the usual pattern has changed, call maternity care immediately. Do not delay for a sweet drink or a two-hour count. No fixed number of movements or a home Doppler can confirm wellbeing when you are concerned.

What symptoms can occur with placental abruption?

Abdominal or back pain, tenderness, frequent contractions and bleeding can occur, but bleeding may be concealed. These symptoms need immediate assessment. Severe pain, heavy bleeding, faintness or collapse requires emergency help; do not wait for all symptoms or drive yourself.

Which infections can be involved in stillbirth?

Examples include bacterial infection of the womb, listeriosis, syphilis, CMV and parvovirus B19, with others relevant to geography or exposure. Not every infection or positive test caused the loss. Timing, treatment and placental or fetal findings must be considered together.

Does a cord around the neck prove why a baby died?

No. A nuchal cord can also occur in an uncomplicated live birth. Specialists look for evidence of impaired blood flow or oxygen supply and consider other causes before assigning a cord-related explanation.

Can a small baby still be healthy?

Yes. Some babies are naturally small. Growth restriction means growth has been limited by a problem and needs assessment, using growth trends and other findings. A single weight measurement alone does not establish placental failure.

Will postmortem or genetic testing always give an answer?

No. These tests can provide useful information but may not establish a definite cause. Ask about the options and consent, what a result could change and when it will be explained. Genetic counselling may be helpful for a relevant result or family history.

Does finding a risk factor mean I could have prevented the loss?

No. A risk factor describes an association, not proof of what happened or what one person could have changed. Ask the team to explain the specific evidence and any future recommendations without blame. Grief support does not depend on finding a cause.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
